question: What is Natural Language Processing (NLP)? What are its main applications?
hinglish_explanation: NLP computers ko human language samajhne aur generate karne ki ability deta hai. Applications: chatbots, translation, sentiment analysis, search, spam detection. Jahan bhi machine ko language samajhni ho wahan NLP lagta hai.
real_life_example: Google Translate, Alexa/Siri, Gmail spam filter, Google Search, Grammarly, ChatGPT - sab NLP use karte hain. Phone keyboard ka autocomplete bhi NLP hai.
how_to_answer: NLP enables machines to understand, interpret, and generate human language
Core tasks: classification, NER, translation, QA, summarization, generation
Two areas: NLU (understanding) and NLG (generation)
Evolution: rule-based → statistical → deep learning → transformers → LLMs
Challenges: ambiguity, context, sarcasm, multilingual
In my work: semantic search, text-to-SQL, RAG pipelines

question: What is tokenization? Why is it the first step in NLP pipelines?
hinglish_explanation: Tokenization text ko chhote units mein todna hai. Models raw text nahi samajhte, numbers chahiye. Modern models BPE/WordPiece use karte hain jo rare words bhi handle karte hain.
real_life_example: 'Don't stop!' → Word: ['Don', "'t", 'stop', '!']. BPE handles unknown words by breaking into subwords. BERT ka WordPiece, GPT ka BPE. Wrong tokenizer = wrong results.
how_to_answer: Tokenization splits text into units models can process
Models need numerical input - tokens mapped to IDs then embeddings
Word-level: simple but OOV problem
Subword (BPE/WordPiece): handles any word via subunits
Modern standard: 30K-50K vocab subword tokenization
Always use tokenizer matching your model
BPE for GPT, WordPiece for BERT, SentencePiece for multilingual

question: What is the difference between stemming and lemmatization?
hinglish_explanation: Stemming crude suffix chop (running→runn). Lemmatization proper root form (running→run, better→good). Modern DL mein dono zaruri nahi - subword tokenization handle karta hai.
real_life_example: 'Studies studying studied' → Stemming: 'studi studi studi'. Lemmatization: 'study study study'. Search engines stemming use karte hain, BERT/GPT ko ye nahi chahiye.
how_to_answer: Stemming: rule-based suffix stripping, fast but may produce non-words
Lemmatization: dictionary-based root form, accurate but slower
Stemming for speed (search engines), lemmatization for accuracy
Modern DL: neither needed - subword tokenization handles morphology
Porter/Snowball stemmers, SpaCy/WordNet lemmatizer
Use in traditional ML pipelines, skip for transformers

question: What are stop words and when should you remove them?
hinglish_explanation: Stop words: 'the', 'is', 'at' - high frequency, low meaning. Traditional NLP mein remove. Modern DL mein REMOVE MAT KARO - transformers ko context chahiye.
real_life_example: 'This is not good' - 'not' remove kiya toh sentiment wrong. TF-IDF ke liye remove OK. BERT ke liye never remove.
how_to_answer: High-frequency words with limited semantic value
Remove for BoW/TF-IDF - reduces noise
DO NOT remove for transformers - context needed
'not','very' carry meaning despite being common
Domain-specific stop words may be needed
My approach: remove for classical ML only

question: What is Bag of Words and what are its limitations?
hinglish_explanation: BoW: document = word counts vector. Order ignore. 'Dog bites man' = 'Man bites dog' (problem!). Simple but misses semantics, order, context.
real_life_example: Spam detection mein BoW works surprisingly well. But 'not good' vs 'good' distinguish nahi kar sakta. TF-IDF BoW se better hai.
how_to_answer: Represents document as word frequency vector
Ignores word order - major limitation
No semantic understanding
High dimensionality, sparse vectors
TF-IDF variant adds importance weighting
Quick baseline before deep learning
CountVectorizer in sklearn implements it

question: How does TF-IDF work and why is it better than raw word counts?
hinglish_explanation: TF-IDF = Term Frequency × Inverse Document Frequency. Rare important words high score, common words low. 'the' low, 'carcinoma' high in medical docs.
real_life_example: Search ranking: 'machine learning Python' - TF-IDF ranks docs where these terms are distinctive. BM25 improved version, still baseline for search.
how_to_answer: TF: word frequency in document, IDF: log(N/df) penalizes common terms
High for discriminative terms, low for common words
Sublinear TF, smooth IDF, L2 normalization variants
BM25: improved TF-IDF with saturation and length normalization
Still competitive baseline for information retrieval
sklearn TfidfVectorizer implements it
My baseline for any text similarity/search task

question: What is text preprocessing and what steps are involved?
hinglish_explanation: Raw text clean karna models ke liye. Traditional: lowercase, punctuation remove, tokenize, stem. Modern DL: minimal preprocessing - sirf tokenization. Over-preprocessing = information loss.
real_life_example: Tweet '@User OMG!! BAD 😡 #worst' - preprocessing depends on task. Sentiment ke liye emojis/caps matter! Don't blindly remove everything.
how_to_answer: Steps: lowercasing, punctuation removal, tokenization, normalization
For classical ML: full pipeline with stemming/stop words
For deep learning: minimal - just tokenization
Don't over-preprocess: casing/punctuation carry signal
Domain-specific: medical/legal needs specialized handling
Always match preprocessing to model requirements

question: What are n-grams in NLP? How are they used?
hinglish_explanation: N-grams: N consecutive words/characters ka group. Unigram (1 word), bigram (2 words), trigram (3 words). 'I love NLP' → bigrams: ['I love', 'love NLP']. Word order thoda capture hota hai BoW se better. Language models mein probability estimate ke liye use hote the.
real_life_example: Spam detection: bigram 'free money' zyada indicative hai than individual 'free' ya 'money'. Autocomplete: trigram model predict karta hai next word given previous 2. Google Ngram Viewer historical word usage track karta hai.
how_to_answer: N-grams: contiguous sequence of N items (words or characters)
Unigram (1), bigram (2), trigram (3) most common
Captures local word order unlike bag-of-words
Used in: language models, text classification features, spelling correction
Character n-grams: robust to typos, useful for language detection
TF-IDF with bigrams often better than unigrams alone
Limitation: exponential vocabulary growth with N, data sparsity

question: What is text classification? What are common approaches?
hinglish_explanation: Text classification: text ko predefined categories mein assign. Spam/not-spam (binary), topic classification (multi-class), tags (multi-label). Approaches: TF-IDF+SVM (traditional), CNN for text, fine-tuned BERT (modern SOTA).
real_life_example: Email spam filter, news categorization (sports/politics/tech), customer support ticket routing, content moderation (toxic/safe). Mere project mein: customer intent classification for chatbot routing.
how_to_answer: Assign predefined labels to text documents
Binary (spam/not), multi-class (topics), multi-label (tags)
Traditional: TF-IDF + Logistic Regression/SVM/Naive Bayes
Deep learning: CNN/LSTM for text, fine-tuned transformers
Transfer learning: BERT fine-tuning is current standard
Evaluation: accuracy, F1, confusion matrix per class
My approach: TF-IDF+LR baseline, upgrade to BERT if needed

question: What is the difference between NLU and NLG?
hinglish_explanation: NLU (Natural Language Understanding): text samajhna - classification, NER, parsing, sentiment. NLG (Natural Language Generation): text produce karna - summarization, translation, chatbot responses. BERT = NLU focused, GPT = NLG focused. Modern LLMs dono kar sakte hain.
real_life_example: NLU: 'Book a flight to Mumbai tomorrow' samajhna (intent: booking, entities: Mumbai, tomorrow). NLG: Response generate karna 'I found 5 flights to Mumbai for tomorrow. Would you like to see options?' Chatbot mein dono chahiye.
how_to_answer: NLU: understanding/comprehension - extracting meaning from text
NLG: generation/production - creating fluent text from data/intent
NLU tasks: classification, NER, parsing, sentiment, QA
NLG tasks: summarization, translation, dialogue, text generation
BERT architecture: encoder-only, designed for NLU tasks
GPT architecture: decoder-only, designed for NLG tasks
T5/BART: encoder-decoder, good at both NLU and NLG

question: What are word embeddings and why are they important in NLP?
hinglish_explanation: Word embeddings words ko dense vectors mein convert karte hain jahan similar words close hote hain. One-hot encoding mein 'king' aur 'queen' equally different hain, but embeddings mein ye close hain. Semantic meaning capture hota hai numbers mein.
real_life_example: Flipkart search mein 'mobile' search karo toh 'smartphone', 'phone', 'cellphone' bhi dikhte hain kyunki embeddings mein ye sab close hain. Without embeddings exact match chahiye hota.
how_to_answer: Dense vector representation of words in continuous space
Similar words have similar vectors - captures semantics
One-hot: sparse, no similarity; Embeddings: dense, semantic relationships
Pre-trained: Word2Vec, GloVe, FastText
Contextual: BERT embeddings change with context
Foundation of modern NLP - all DL models use them
Typical dimensions: 100-768 depending on model

question: What is text similarity and how can it be measured?
hinglish_explanation: Do texts kitne similar hain ye measure karna. Cosine similarity sabse common - angle measure karta hai vectors ke beech. Jaccard simple word overlap dekhta hai. Semantic similarity meaning compare karti hai, lexical sirf words compare karti hai.
real_life_example: Quora duplicate question detection - 'How to learn Python?' aur 'Best way to start Python?' same intent hai. Flipkart mein similar products group karna. Resume-job matching bhi text similarity hai.
how_to_answer: Lexical: exact/near word overlap (Jaccard, edit distance)
Semantic: meaning-based (cosine similarity on embeddings)
Cosine similarity: dot product / (norm1 * norm2), range [-1,1]
TF-IDF + cosine for traditional approach
Sentence-BERT for modern semantic similarity
BM25 for retrieval, cross-encoder for re-ranking
Task-dependent: choose metric based on use case

question: What is regex and how is it used in NLP?
hinglish_explanation: Regex (Regular Expressions) pattern matching ka tool hai text mein. Email extract karna, phone numbers dhundhna, dates parse karna - sab regex se hota hai. NLP preprocessing mein bahut kaam aata hai especially rule-based systems mein.
real_life_example: Banking app mein account number extract karna messages se: regex pattern '\d{10,12}' 10-12 digit numbers dhundh leta hai. OTP extraction bhi regex se hoti hai - '\b\d{4,6}\b' pattern.
how_to_answer: Pattern matching tool for text - find, extract, replace
Common NLP uses: tokenization, cleaning, entity extraction
Patterns: \d (digit), \w (word char), \s (space), . (any)
Quantifiers: * (0+), + (1+), ? (0-1), {n} (exactly n)
Groups () for extraction, | for alternation
Fast for rule-based extraction before ML
Combine with ML: regex for obvious patterns, ML for complex

question: What is language detection and how does it work?
hinglish_explanation: Text kis language mein hai ye identify karna. Character n-grams use hote hain mostly - har language ke unique character patterns hote hain. 'the' English mein common, 'der/die/das' German mein. Short text mein tricky hota hai.
real_life_example: Google Translate auto-detect feature. Twitter pe multilingual posts classify karna. Customer support mein Hindi vs English query alag agents ko route karna. Indian context mein Hinglish detection tough hai.
how_to_answer: Identify the language of given text
Character n-gram frequency analysis most effective
Libraries: langdetect, fasttext-langdetect, polyglot
Short text (<20 chars) is challenging
Script-based: Devanagari=Hindi, Arabic script=Urdu/Arabic
Challenges: code-mixed text (Hinglish), transliteration
fastText's lid.176.bin covers 176 languages

question: What is spell checking in NLP and what algorithms are used?
hinglish_explanation: Galat spelling detect aur correct karna. Edit distance (Levenshtein) measure karta hai kitne changes chahiye ek word ko dusre mein convert karne ke liye. Peter Norvig ka simple spell corrector bahut famous hai - word probability + edit distance use karta hai.
real_life_example: Google 'Did you mean?' feature. WhatsApp autocorrect. Grammarly suggestions. Indian names ke liye standard spell checkers fail hote hain - custom dictionary chahiye.
how_to_answer: Detect and correct misspelled words in text
Edit distance (Levenshtein): insertions, deletions, substitutions
Noisy channel model: P(correction|misspelling) ∝ P(misspelling|correction) × P(correction)
Peter Norvig's algorithm: generate candidates within edit distance 1-2
Context-aware: BERT-based models consider surrounding words
Challenges: proper nouns, domain terms, code-mixed text
Libraries: pyspellchecker, SymSpell (fastest), hunspell

question: What is text normalization and why is it needed?
hinglish_explanation: Text ko standard form mein lana. '2morrow', 'tmrw', 'tomorrow' sab same hain. Numbers ko words mein, abbreviations expand, unicode normalize - sab text normalization hai. Consistency chahiye models ko.
real_life_example: Social media analysis: 'gr8', 'great', 'GREAT', 'greatttt' sab same meaning. Customer reviews mein 'Rs.', 'INR', '₹' normalize karna. Dates: '15/01/2024', 'Jan 15, 2024', '15th January' sab same.
how_to_answer: Converting text to consistent standard form
Steps: lowercasing, unicode normalization, expanding contractions
Number normalization: digits to words or vice versa
Abbreviation expansion: 'govt' → 'government'
Social media: 'gr8'→'great', 'u'→'you'
Important for: search, deduplication, feature extraction
Balance: normalize enough but don't lose meaning

question: What is a corpus and vocabulary in NLP context?
hinglish_explanation: Corpus: text data ka collection jis pe model train hota hai. Wikipedia corpus, news corpus, etc. Vocabulary: unique words/tokens ka set jo corpus mein hain. Vocab size model complexity decide karta hai. OOV (Out of Vocabulary) words problem hoti hai.
real_life_example: BERT ka corpus: English Wikipedia + BooksCorpus (3.3B words). Hindi NLP ke liye IIT Bombay Hindi corpus. Banking chatbot ke liye banking documents ka corpus banana padta hai domain-specific performance ke liye.
how_to_answer: Corpus: collection of text documents used for training/evaluation
Vocabulary: set of unique tokens in the corpus
Corpus types: monolingual, parallel, domain-specific
Vocab size: tradeoff - larger captures more but slower
OOV handling: subword tokenization (BPE), <UNK> token
Common corpora: Wikipedia, Common Crawl, BookCorpus
Domain corpus curation crucial for specialized NLP

question: What is Named Entity Recognition (NER)?
hinglish_explanation: Text mein entities identify karna - person names, locations, organizations, dates, money amounts. Sequence labeling task hai - har token ko label assign (B-PER, I-PER, O). SpaCy, BERT-based NER models use hote hain.
real_life_example: News article se automatically extract: Person='Narendra Modi', Location='Delhi', Organization='BJP', Date='15 August 2024'. Banking mein transaction messages se amount, merchant, date extract karna NER hai.
how_to_answer: Identify and classify named entities in text
Entity types: PERSON, ORG, LOCATION, DATE, MONEY, etc.
Tagging scheme: BIO (Begin, Inside, Outside)
Approaches: rule-based, CRF, BiLSTM-CRF, BERT fine-tuning
SpaCy for quick NER, HuggingFace for custom training
Domain-specific NER needs custom training data
Evaluation: entity-level F1 (exact match + type match)

question: What is sentiment analysis and what are its types?
hinglish_explanation: Text ka sentiment (positive/negative/neutral) determine karna. Binary (pos/neg), ternary (+neutral), fine-grained (1-5 stars), aspect-based (food:positive, service:negative). Sarcasm detect karna mushkil hai!
real_life_example: Zomato/Swiggy reviews analyze: 'Food was amazing but delivery took forever' - aspect-based sentiment: food=positive, delivery=negative. Brand monitoring: Twitter pe company ke baare mein log kya bol rahe hain.
how_to_answer: Determine emotional tone/opinion in text
Types: binary, ternary, fine-grained (1-5), aspect-based
Aspect-based: different sentiment for different aspects
Approaches: lexicon-based (VADER), ML (SVM), DL (BERT)
Challenges: sarcasm, negation, implicit sentiment
VADER for quick analysis, fine-tuned BERT for accuracy
Real application: product reviews, social media monitoring

question: What is Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging?
hinglish_explanation: Har word ko uska grammatical role assign karna - noun, verb, adjective, etc. 'The cat sat on the mat' → DET NOUN VERB ADP DET NOUN. Downstream tasks ke liye useful: NER, parsing, information extraction. Modern models mein implicit hota hai.
real_life_example: Grammar checker mein POS tagging use hota hai - 'He go market' mein 'go' verb hai but subject 'He' singular hai toh 'goes' suggest karo. SpaCy ek line mein POS tags de deta hai.
how_to_answer: Assign grammatical category to each word in sentence
Tags: NOUN, VERB, ADJ, ADV, DET, PREP, CONJ, etc.
Penn Treebank tagset (45 tags) most common
Approaches: rule-based, HMM, CRF, neural (BiLSTM)
SpaCy, NLTK, Stanza provide POS tagging
Used as feature for NER, parsing, text-to-speech
Modern transformers learn POS implicitly

question: What is the difference between rule-based and statistical NLP?
hinglish_explanation: Rule-based: manually written rules (if word='not' then negate). Statistical: data se patterns seekhna. Rule-based predictable but limited, statistical flexible but needs data. Modern: statistical (ML/DL) dominate karta hai, rules for preprocessing.
real_life_example: Email filtering: Rule-based='Block if contains Nigeria+prince+money'. Statistical=Train model on 1000s of spam/ham emails. Statistical better kyunki new spam patterns bhi catch karta hai jo rules miss karte hain.
how_to_answer: Rule-based: handcrafted patterns, regex, grammars, dictionaries
Statistical: learn patterns from data (ML/DL models)
Rule-based: precise, interpretable but brittle, limited coverage
Statistical: flexible, generalizable but needs data, less interpretable
Hybrid approach often best: rules for known patterns, ML for rest
Evolution: rules (1950s-80s) → statistical (1990s-2010s) → deep learning (2010s+)
Current trend: pre-trained LLMs with minimal rules

question: What is text encoding and why does it matter in NLP?
hinglish_explanation: Computers text ko bytes mein store karte hain. UTF-8 sabse common encoding hai jo multilingual text handle karta hai. Wrong encoding = garbled text (mojibake). Hindi/Chinese text ke liye UTF-8 must hai. ASCII sirf English handle karta hai.
real_life_example: Indian banking apps mein Hindi SMS garbled dikhte hain agar encoding wrong hai. Web scraping mein encoding mismatch se '?' ya weird characters aate hain. Always use UTF-8 for Indian language NLP.
how_to_answer: Text encoding maps characters to bytes for computer storage
ASCII: 128 chars, English only
UTF-8: variable-length, supports all Unicode characters
UTF-8 is standard for NLP - handles multilingual text
Common issues: mojibake from encoding mismatch
Always specify encoding when reading files: open(f, encoding='utf-8')
Preprocessing step: detect and normalize encoding

question: What is the curse of dimensionality in text representation?
hinglish_explanation: Vocabulary bada = vector bada = computation mushkil. 100K words ka one-hot vector sparse hai mostly zeros. Distance metrics meaningless ho jaate hain high dimensions mein. Dimensionality reduction ya dense embeddings solution hain.
real_life_example: E-commerce: 50K products, 100K unique words in descriptions. BoW matrix = 50K × 100K = 5 billion entries (mostly 0). Memory aur speed problem. Embeddings: 50K × 300 = 15M entries (manageable).
how_to_answer: High-dimensional sparse representations cause computational issues
One-hot/BoW: vocab-size dimensions, mostly zeros
Distance metrics become meaningless in very high dimensions
Solutions: dimensionality reduction (PCA, SVD), dense embeddings
Word embeddings: 100-300 dims vs 100K+ for one-hot
Topic models (LDA) reduce document dimensions
Modern: pre-trained embeddings avoid this entirely

question: What is the difference between syntax and semantics in NLP?
hinglish_explanation: Syntax = grammar/structure (sentence grammatically correct hai ya nahi). Semantics = meaning (sentence ka matlab kya hai). 'Colorless green ideas sleep furiously' - syntactically correct but semantically nonsense. NLP ko dono handle karna padta hai.
real_life_example: Chatbot mein: syntax check karega ki user ne valid sentence likha, semantics samjhega ki user kya chahta hai. 'Book a flight' vs 'Flight a book' - syntax different, ek meaningful ek nahi.
how_to_answer: Syntax: grammatical structure, word order, sentence formation
Semantics: meaning, interpretation, understanding
Syntactic analysis: POS tagging, parsing, grammar checking
Semantic analysis: word sense disambiguation, sentiment, NLU
'Time flies like an arrow' - syntactically simple, semantically ambiguous
Transformers capture both via self-attention mechanism
Syntax = form, Semantics = function

question: What is word sense disambiguation (WSD)?
hinglish_explanation: Ek word ke multiple meanings mein se correct meaning identify karna context ke basis pe. 'Bank' = river bank ya financial bank? 'Apple' = fruit ya company? Context dekhke decide karna padta hai. BERT naturally ye kar leta hai contextual embeddings se.
real_life_example: Search engine: 'Java' search karo - programming language ya island ya coffee? Context clues se decide: 'Java programming tutorial' vs 'Java island tourism'. Google ye WSD use karta hai results improve karne ke liye.
how_to_answer: Determine correct meaning of ambiguous words using context
Polysemy: one word, multiple meanings (bank, bat, crane)
Approaches: knowledge-based (WordNet), supervised ML, neural
Lesk algorithm: overlap between context and dictionary definition
BERT/contextual embeddings: naturally disambiguate via context
Different embedding for 'bank' in 'river bank' vs 'bank account'
Critical for: MT, IR, QA systems

question: How does Word2Vec work? Explain CBOW and Skip-gram architectures.
hinglish_explanation: Word2Vec 2 architectures hai: CBOW context words se center word predict karta hai, Skip-gram center word se context words predict karta hai. Shallow neural network hai - input→hidden→output. Training ke baad hidden layer weights = word embeddings. Skip-gram rare words ke liye better, CBOW fast hai.
real_life_example: 'The cat sat on the ___' - CBOW 'mat' predict karega context se. Skip-gram: 'sat' diya toh 'cat', 'on', 'the' predict karega. Google ne 2013 mein release kiya tha, NLP mein revolution aa gaya tha.
how_to_answer: Word2Vec: neural network that learns word vectors from context
CBOW: predict center word from surrounding context words
Skip-gram: predict context words from center word
Architecture: input(one-hot) → hidden(embedding) → output(softmax)
Skip-gram better for rare words, CBOW faster for frequent
Negative sampling: approximate softmax for efficiency
Hyperparameters: embedding dim (100-300), window size (5-10)

question: What is GloVe and how does it differ from Word2Vec?
hinglish_explanation: GloVe (Global Vectors) co-occurrence matrix factorize karta hai. Word2Vec local context window dekhta hai, GloVe global statistics (puri corpus ki word-word co-occurrence counts) use karta hai. Dono similar quality embeddings dete hain but training approach different hai.
real_life_example: Stanford ne GloVe banaya. Wikipedia+Gigaword pe trained 6B tokens version free available hai. Practice mein Word2Vec aur GloVe similar perform karte hain - FastText dono se better hai OOV handling mein.
how_to_answer: GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation (Stanford 2014)
Combines count-based (LSA) and prediction-based (Word2Vec) approaches
Builds word co-occurrence matrix from corpus
Factorizes log co-occurrence matrix to get embeddings
Word2Vec: local context windows; GloVe: global corpus statistics
Training: weighted least squares on co-occurrence counts
Performance similar to Word2Vec, different training paradigm

question: What is FastText and how does it handle out-of-vocabulary words?
hinglish_explanation: FastText (Facebook) word ko character n-grams mein todta hai aur unke embeddings sum karta hai. 'where' = '<wh', 'whe', 'her', 'ere', 're>' + '<where>'. New/misspelled words ke liye bhi embedding generate kar sakta hai character n-grams se. Word2Vec/GloVe ye nahi kar sakte.
real_life_example: Indian names jaise 'Priyanka' training mein nahi hai but 'Pri', 'riy', 'iya', 'yan', 'ank', 'nka' subwords se reasonable embedding mil jaata hai. Typos handle: 'amazng' bhi 'amazing' ke close embedding dega.
how_to_answer: FastText: extension of Word2Vec with character n-grams
Each word = sum of its character n-gram vectors
Handles OOV: compose embedding from subword pieces
Better for morphologically rich languages (Hindi, Turkish)
Handles typos and rare words gracefully
Available in 157 languages pre-trained
Faster training than Word2Vec with subword information

question: How do you evaluate word embeddings?
hinglish_explanation: Intrinsic evaluation: analogy tasks (king-man+woman=queen), similarity benchmarks (WordSim-353). Extrinsic evaluation: downstream task pe performance (NER, classification). Best evaluation = apne actual task pe try karo. Analogy tasks overrated hain.
real_life_example: Google analogy dataset: 'Delhi:India :: Tokyo:?' answer 'Japan' hona chahiye. SimLex-999 human similarity ratings se compare karo. But ultimately apne use case pe test karo - embedding jo analogy ace kare wo zaruri nahi classification mein best ho.
how_to_answer: Intrinsic: word analogy tasks (a:b :: c:?), similarity correlation
Extrinsic: performance on downstream tasks (NER, classification)
Analogy: king-man+woman=queen, captures relationships
Similarity benchmarks: WordSim-353, SimLex-999, MEN
Visualization: t-SNE/UMAP to check clustering quality
Bias detection: gender/racial bias in embeddings
Best practice: evaluate on YOUR specific task

question: What are word embedding analogies and how do they work?
hinglish_explanation: Vector arithmetic se relationships capture hote hain. vec('king') - vec('man') + vec('woman') ≈ vec('queen'). Direction 'man→king' same hai 'woman→queen'. Linear relationships encode hoti hain embedding space mein. But ye perfect nahi hai - cherry-picked examples famous hain.
real_life_example: 'India':'Delhi' :: 'Japan':'Tokyo' - capital city relationship. 'big':'bigger' :: 'small':'smaller' - comparative form. Practical use limited hai but concept demonstrates ki embeddings semantic relationships capture karte hain.
how_to_answer: Vector arithmetic captures semantic relationships
a:b :: c:d means vec(b)-vec(a)+vec(c) ≈ vec(d)
Types: syntactic (run:running), semantic (king:queen), geographic
Demonstrates embeddings capture linear relationships
Evaluation: Google analogy dataset (19K questions)
Limitations: works for some relations, fails for others
Not cherry-pick: accuracy typically 60-75% on full dataset

question: How do you visualize word embeddings?
hinglish_explanation: 300-dim vectors ko 2D/3D mein project karna visualization ke liye. t-SNE non-linear method hai jo local structure preserve karta hai - clusters dikhata hai. UMAP faster hai aur global structure bhi better preserve karta hai. TensorFlow Embedding Projector interactive tool hai.
real_life_example: Product embeddings visualize karke dekho ki similar products cluster hote hain ya nahi. t-SNE plot mein shoes ek cluster, electronics alag cluster. Quality check ke liye useful hai - agar 'good' aur 'bad' same cluster mein hain toh embedding kharab hai.
how_to_answer: Dimensionality reduction: high-dim → 2D/3D for plotting
t-SNE: non-linear, preserves local neighborhood structure
UMAP: faster, preserves both local and global structure
PCA: linear, fast but may miss non-linear relationships
TensorFlow Embedding Projector: interactive web tool
Use for: quality check, cluster verification, debugging
Perplexity (t-SNE) and n_neighbors (UMAP) are key hyperparameters

question: What is negative sampling in Word2Vec?
hinglish_explanation: Full softmax over entire vocab (100K+ words) expensive hai. Negative sampling: correct word ke saath randomly kuch galat words pick karo aur sirf unke against train karo. 5-20 negative samples enough hain. Training 100x fast ho jaati hai quality sacrifice ke bina.
real_life_example: 'The cat sat on the ___' - correct: 'mat'. Instead of computing probability over 100K words, sirf 'mat' (positive) vs randomly picked 'elephant','democracy','purple' (negatives) pe train karo. Bahut faster!
how_to_answer: Approximation technique for efficient Word2Vec training
Full softmax: compute over entire vocabulary - too expensive
Negative sampling: train on correct pair + K random negative pairs
K=5-20 negative samples works well in practice
Negatives sampled by word frequency (raised to 0.75 power)
Converts multi-class to binary classification
NCE (Noise Contrastive Estimation) is theoretical foundation

question: What is the effect of embedding dimensions on performance?
hinglish_explanation: Dimension = kitne numbers se ek word represent hoga. Kam dims (50): fast but less expressive. Zyada dims (300-768): richer representation but more compute. Sweet spot usually 100-300 hai word embeddings ke liye. BERT 768 use karta hai. Diminishing returns after a point.
real_life_example: Small dataset (10K docs): 100 dims enough. Large corpus (Wikipedia): 300 dims better. Mobile app: 50 dims for speed. Research: 768-1024 dims for best quality. Tradeoff: memory vs quality. Production mein often 256 dims best balance.
how_to_answer: Embedding dimension: number of features per word vector
Small dims (50-100): faster, less memory, sufficient for small vocab
Medium dims (200-300): standard for Word2Vec/GloVe
Large dims (768-1024): transformer models, rich representations
Diminishing returns: beyond 300, marginal improvement
Rule of thumb: 4th root of vocab size as minimum dimension
Task-dependent: simple tasks need fewer dims

question: What is subword tokenization and why did it replace word-level tokenization?
hinglish_explanation: Words ko smaller meaningful pieces mein todna. 'unhappiness' → 'un', 'happi', 'ness'. Fixed vocab size ke saath infinite words handle. BPE (GPT), WordPiece (BERT), Unigram (XLNet) teen main algorithms hain. OOV problem completely solve ho gayi.
real_life_example: Indian languages: 'खुशियाँ' agar vocab mein nahi hai toh subwords 'खुश' + 'ियाँ' mein tod do. English: 'COVID-19' 2019 mein kisi vocab mein nahi tha but subwords se handle ho gaya: 'CO', 'VID', '-', '19'.
how_to_answer: Tokenize words into subword units instead of full words
Solves OOV problem: any word composed from subword vocab
BPE: iteratively merge most frequent character pairs
WordPiece: merge pairs that maximize language model likelihood
Unigram: probabilistic, starts large vocab and prunes
Fixed vocab size (30K-50K) covers virtually all text
Morphologically aware: captures prefixes, suffixes, roots

question: What are contextual embeddings and how do they differ from static embeddings?
hinglish_explanation: Static (Word2Vec/GloVe): ek word ka ek hi vector hamesha. 'bank' ka same vector chahe river bank ho ya money bank. Contextual (ELMo/BERT): surrounding words ke basis pe vector change hota hai. Same word, different contexts = different embeddings. Much more powerful!
real_life_example: 'Apple is delicious' vs 'Apple launched iPhone' - static embedding mein 'Apple' same vector. BERT mein first wala fruit cluster mein, second wala tech company cluster mein. Context-aware representation se accuracy significantly improve hoti hai.
how_to_answer: Static: one fixed vector per word regardless of context (Word2Vec, GloVe)
Contextual: embedding changes based on surrounding words (ELMo, BERT, GPT)
Static: 'bank' has same vector in all contexts
Contextual: 'bank' near finance words vs river words = different vectors
ELMo: first contextual embeddings (BiLSTM-based, 2018)
BERT: transformer-based contextual embeddings (2018)
Contextual embeddings dominate all NLP benchmarks now

question: What is the window size parameter in Word2Vec and how does it affect embeddings?
hinglish_explanation: Window size = center word ke kitne aas-paas ke words context mein consider karne hain. Small window (2-3): syntactic relationships capture (adjective-noun). Large window (8-10): semantic/topical relationships (doctor-hospital). Task ke hisaab se tune karo.
real_life_example: Window=2: 'good' ke paas 'very', 'great' aayenge (syntactic similarity). Window=10: 'doctor' ke paas 'hospital', 'patient', 'medicine' aayenge (topic similarity). Analogy tasks ke liye larger window better hai.
how_to_answer: Window size: number of surrounding words considered as context
Small window (2-5): captures syntactic/functional similarity
Large window (5-15): captures semantic/topical similarity
Symmetric window: equal words left and right
Dynamic window: randomly sample size between 1 and max
Larger window = more training pairs but noisier signal
Default 5 works well for most applications

question: How does ELMo generate contextual word representations?
hinglish_explanation: ELMo (Embeddings from Language Models) 2-layer BiLSTM language model hai. Forward LM left-to-right, backward LM right-to-left padta hai. Har layer ka output combine karta hai weighted sum se. Task-specific weights learn hote hain. BERT se pehle SOTA tha.
real_life_example: ELMo ne 2018 mein sab NLP benchmarks pe SOTA achieve kiya tha. Existing model ke upar ELMo features add kardo = instant improvement. Lekin ab BERT ne replace kar diya hai - BERT ka contextual representation better hai.
how_to_answer: ELMo: Embeddings from Language Models (AllenNLP, 2018)
Architecture: 2-layer BiLSTM trained as language model
Forward + backward LM gives contextual representations
Final embedding: weighted sum of all BiLSTM layers
Different layers capture different info (syntax vs semantics)
Task-specific layer weights are learnable parameters
Limitation: shallow bidirectionality, BERT replaced it

question: What is the difference between pre-trained and custom-trained embeddings?
hinglish_explanation: Pre-trained: Google/Stanford ne large corpus pe train kiye (Wikipedia). Custom: apne domain data pe khud train karo. Medical/legal/finance domain mein custom better kyunki general embeddings mein 'stat' = statistics but medical mein 'stat' = immediately.
real_life_example: Flipkart product search: pre-trained embeddings mein 'kurta' aur 'kurti' close nahi honge. Custom embeddings Flipkart catalog pe train karo toh similar products cluster properly honge. Domain matters!
how_to_answer: Pre-trained: trained on large general corpus (Wikipedia, news)
Custom: trained on domain-specific data
Pre-trained advantages: quick start, broad coverage, proven quality
Custom advantages: domain terminology, specific relationships
Approach: start with pre-trained, fine-tune on domain data
Domain-specific terms often poorly represented in general embeddings
Hybrid: initialize with pre-trained, continue training on domain

question: What is the Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) algorithm for tokenization?
hinglish_explanation: BPE iteratively most frequent character pairs merge karta hai. Start: individual characters. Step 1: sabse common pair merge (e.g., 't'+'h'='th'). Repeat until vocab size reach ho. Result: common words intact, rare words subwords mein. GPT family BPE use karti hai.
real_life_example: Vocab building: 'low','lower','lowest','new','newer','newest' → BPE learns: 'low', 'er', 'est', 'new' as subwords. 'newer' = 'new'+'er'. Unseen 'lowest' = 'low'+'est'. Efficient vocab with full coverage.
how_to_answer: BPE: iteratively merge most frequent adjacent symbol pairs
Start with character-level vocabulary
Each iteration: find most frequent pair, create new symbol
Stop when desired vocab size reached
Handles any word through subword composition
GPT-2/3/4 use BPE tokenization
Training: learn merges from corpus; Inference: apply learned merges

question: How does WordPiece tokenization differ from BPE?
hinglish_explanation: BPE frequency se merge karta hai, WordPiece likelihood se. WordPiece wo pair merge karta hai jisse language model probability maximize ho. Subtle difference but WordPiece theoretically better choices karta hai. BERT WordPiece use karta hai. '##' prefix subword indicate karta hai.
real_life_example: BERT tokenizer: 'playing' → ['play', '##ing']. '##' matlab ye previous token ka continuation hai. 'Hyderabad' → ['Hy', '##dera', '##bad']. WordPiece BERT ke saath standard ban gaya hai.
how_to_answer: WordPiece: merge pairs that maximize language model likelihood
BPE merges by frequency, WordPiece by likelihood gain
Used by BERT, DistilBERT and related models
Subword prefix '##' indicates continuation of previous token
Vocab size typically 30K for BERT
Greedy longest-match-first tokenization at inference
Difference from BPE is in training objective, not tokenization

question: What is embedding bias and how can it be mitigated?
hinglish_explanation: Embeddings training data ke biases inherit karte hain. 'Doctor' male ke close, 'nurse' female ke close - ye societal bias reflect karta hai. Debiasing techniques: projection-based removal, counterfactual data augmentation. Important for fair AI systems.
real_life_example: Google Translate: Turkish gender-neutral 'o' ko 'he is a doctor', 'she is a nurse' translate karta tha - embedding bias ki wajah se. Amazon ka resume screener ne female candidates ko penalize kiya tha biased embeddings ki wajah se.
how_to_answer: Word embeddings capture societal biases from training data
Gender bias: 'programmer' closer to 'man', 'homemaker' to 'woman'
Racial bias: names associated with different sentiments
Debiasing: identify bias direction, project it out
Hard debiasing (Bolukbasi): neutralize and equalize
Counterfactual Data Augmentation (CDA): balance training data
Continuous challenge: debiasing may reduce and not eliminate bias

question: How do you handle out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words?
hinglish_explanation: OOV = training mein nahi dikha word. Solutions: (1) subword tokenization (best), (2) character-level model, (3) FastText subword embeddings, (4) <UNK> token (worst). Modern models mein OOV problem almost solved hai subword tokenization se.
real_life_example: New slang 'FOMO' ya 'COVID' launch hua - Word2Vec mein OOV. FastText 'COVID' = 'CO'+'VI'+'ID' subwords se approximate embedding dega. BPE/WordPiece: ['CO', 'VID'] tokens generate karega. Problem solved!
how_to_answer: OOV: words not in model's vocabulary during inference
Solutions ranked: subword tokenization > FastText > character-level > UNK
Subword (BPE/WordPiece): any word = composition of known subwords
FastText: character n-gram vectors sum to approximate OOV word
Character-level CNN/LSTM: build word representation from characters
UNK token: last resort, loses all semantic information
Prevention: use large diverse training corpus, subword tokenization

question: What is SentencePiece and why is it used for multilingual models?
hinglish_explanation: SentencePiece language-agnostic tokenizer hai. Raw text pe directly kaam karta hai bina pre-tokenization ke. Spaces bhi special character (▁) se handle karta hai. Multilingual models (mBERT, XLM-R, T5) ke liye perfect hai kyunki kisi bhi script pe kaam karta hai bina language-specific rules ke.
real_life_example: Hindi, Chinese, Japanese mein spaces differently work karti hain. SentencePiece ko koi fark nahi - raw bytes pe BPE/Unigram apply karta hai. T5 aur LLaMA SentencePiece use karte hain. Devanagari script bhi cleanly tokenize hoti hai.
how_to_answer: Language-agnostic tokenization library by Google
Works on raw text without pre-tokenization
Treats space as special symbol (▁) - fully reversible
Supports BPE and Unigram models
Perfect for multilingual: no language-specific rules needed
Handles any script: Latin, Devanagari, CJK, Arabic
Used by: T5, ALBERT, XLNet, LLaMA, mBART

question: What is transfer learning in the context of word embeddings?
hinglish_explanation: Ek task pe seekha hua knowledge dusre task pe use karna. Pre-trained embeddings use karna transfer learning hai. Word2Vec Wikipedia pe train hua, tum apne sentiment classifier mein use karo = transfer learning. Fine-tuning BERT bhi transfer learning hai - general knowledge → specific task.
real_life_example: Startup ke paas sirf 1000 labeled reviews hain. Scratch se embedding train = poor quality. Pre-trained GloVe embeddings use karo = instantly better kyunki Wikipedia ka knowledge transfer ho raha hai. BERT fine-tuning = extreme transfer learning.
how_to_answer: Using knowledge from one task/domain to improve another
Word embeddings: pre-trained on large corpus, used in downstream tasks
Feature-based: use embeddings as fixed features (Word2Vec in classifier)
Fine-tuning: update pre-trained weights on task data (BERT fine-tuning)
Reduces data needs: pre-trained knowledge compensates for small datasets
Evolution: word embeddings → ELMo → BERT → GPT (increasing transfer)
Almost all modern NLP uses transfer learning via pre-trained models

question: What is the relationship between word embeddings and the distributional hypothesis?
hinglish_explanation: Distributional hypothesis: 'You shall know a word by the company it keeps' (Firth, 1957). Jo words similar context mein appear hote hain, unka meaning similar hota hai. Word2Vec/GloVe isi principle pe kaam karte hain - co-occurrence patterns se meaning learn karte hain.
real_life_example: 'chai' aur 'coffee' similar contexts mein aate hain: 'I want ___', 'a cup of ___', '___ with milk'. Isliye embeddings mein close hain. Agar do words hamesha same type ke sentences mein aate hain = similar meaning. Simple yet powerful!
how_to_answer: Distributional hypothesis: words in similar contexts have similar meanings
Firth (1957): 'know a word by the company it keeps'
Foundation of all embedding methods: Word2Vec, GloVe, BERT
Word2Vec: learn from local context windows
GloVe: learn from global co-occurrence statistics
BERT: learn from masked word prediction in context
Limitation: distributional ≠ full meaning (no grounding in real world)

question: What is Doc2Vec and how does it extend Word2Vec?
hinglish_explanation: Doc2Vec Word2Vec ka extension hai documents ke liye. Paragraph vector add hota hai jo document-level context capture karta hai. DM (Distributed Memory) = CBOW + doc vector. DBOW (Distributed Bag of Words) = Skip-gram + doc vector. Variable length documents ka fixed-size representation milta hai.
real_life_example: Flipkart pe product descriptions compare karna - Doc2Vec har product ka fixed-size vector deta hai. Similar products ke vectors close honge. Document clustering, plagiarism detection mein use hota hai.
how_to_answer: Doc2Vec: learns fixed-size vectors for variable-length documents
Extension of Word2Vec with paragraph/document vector
DM (PV-DM): predict word from context + document vector
DBOW (PV-DBOW): predict words from document vector alone
Training: document vector updated during training like word vectors
Inference: freeze word vectors, learn new doc vector for unseen document
Use cases: document similarity, clustering, classification

question: What are sentence embeddings and how are they generated?
hinglish_explanation: Full sentence ka single vector representation. Methods: (1) word embeddings average (simple), (2) TF-IDF weighted average, (3) Sentence-BERT (SOTA), (4) Universal Sentence Encoder. Good sentence embeddings semantic similarity accurately capture karte hain.
real_life_example: Semantic search: user query 'how to return product' ka embedding, FAQ answers ke embeddings se compare. Closest FAQ answer = best response. Swiggy customer support automation aise hi kaam karta hai.
how_to_answer: Fixed-size vector representing entire sentence meaning
Simple: average word embeddings (surprisingly competitive)
TF-IDF weighted average: weight important words more
InferSent: supervised BiLSTM trained on NLI data
Sentence-BERT: fine-tuned BERT with siamese architecture
Universal Sentence Encoder (USE): Google's general-purpose encoder
Choice depends on: speed vs quality tradeoff, task requirements

question: What is the Universal Sentence Encoder (USE)?
hinglish_explanation: Google ka pre-trained model jo sentence ko 512-dim vector mein convert karta hai. Do variants: Transformer-based (accurate) aur DAN-based (fast). TensorFlow Hub se directly use kar sakte ho. General purpose hai - similarity, classification, clustering sab ke liye.
real_life_example: FAQ bot banana hai 100 questions ke liye. USE se sab questions encode karo. User ka question encode karo. Cosine similarity se closest FAQ match karo. 5 lines of code mein working FAQ bot! TF Hub se load karo bus.
how_to_answer: Google's pre-trained sentence embedding model
Output: 512-dimensional sentence vector
Two variants: Transformer (accurate) and DAN (fast/lightweight)
Trained on variety of data: Wikipedia, web news, QA forums
Available via TensorFlow Hub - easy to use
Good for: semantic similarity, clustering, classification
Multilingual version (USE-multilingual) supports 16 languages

question: What is Sentence-BERT and why is it needed over vanilla BERT?
hinglish_explanation: Vanilla BERT se sentence similarity nikalna extremely slow hai - N sentences ke liye N² BERT forward passes chahiye (10K sentences = 65 hours!). Sentence-BERT siamese network use karta hai jo independent sentence embeddings deta hai. Cosine similarity directly compare kar sakte ho. 10K sentences = 5 seconds!
real_life_example: Semantic search with 1M documents: BERT se 1M comparisons = impossible. SBERT se sab documents pre-encode karo (one-time), query encode karo, cosine similarity = milliseconds mein results. Pinecone/Weaviate vector databases SBERT embeddings store karte hain.
how_to_answer: SBERT: Sentence-BERT with siamese/triplet network fine-tuning
Problem with BERT: comparing N sentences needs N² forward passes
SBERT: encode sentences independently, compare with cosine
Architecture: BERT + pooling → fixed-size sentence embedding
Training: siamese network on NLI (entailment/contradiction pairs)
1000x faster than cross-encoder BERT for similarity
Standard for: semantic search, clustering, duplicate detection

question: What are the different pooling strategies for creating sentence embeddings from token embeddings?
hinglish_explanation: BERT har token ka embedding deta hai. Sentence embedding banane ke liye pool karna padta hai. CLS token, mean pooling (average of all tokens), max pooling options hain. Mean pooling generally best results deta hai. CLS token bhi common hai but fine-tuning ke bina weak.
real_life_example: BERT se 'I love this product' ke 6 token embeddings mile. Mean pool: sab ka average = sentence vector. CLS pool: sirf [CLS] token ka vector. Max pool: har dimension ka max across tokens. Sentence-BERT mean pooling recommend karta hai.
how_to_answer: Aggregating token-level embeddings into sentence-level
CLS token pooling: use [CLS] token embedding as sentence representation
Mean pooling: average all token embeddings (often best)
Max pooling: element-wise maximum across all tokens
Weighted mean: attention-weighted average of tokens
CLS without fine-tuning often worse than mean pooling
SBERT default: mean pooling over all output tokens

question: What is the difference between contextualized and static text representations?
hinglish_explanation: Static: Word2Vec/GloVe - ek word = ek vector hamesha (context ignore). Contextualized: BERT/GPT - same word different contexts mein different vector. 'I went to the bank' - financial context mein vs river context mein 'bank' ka vector different hoga BERT mein. Massive improvement in NLP tasks.
real_life_example: Product review: 'The phone is not bad' - static mein 'bad' negative embedding. BERT mein 'not bad' context dekhke positive-ish representation. Negation handling bahut better hota hai contextual embeddings se.
how_to_answer: Static: same vector regardless of context (Word2Vec, GloVe, FastText)
Contextualized: different vector for each usage (BERT, GPT, ELMo)
Static captures word-level semantics only
Contextualized captures word + sentence-level meaning
Polysemy handling: contextual solves it, static cannot
Static: fast, small memory; Contextual: slower, more memory
Modern NLP: always prefer contextualized unless resource-constrained

question: What is Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) and how does it work?
hinglish_explanation: LSA term-document matrix pe SVD (Singular Value Decomposition) apply karta hai dimensionality reduce karne ke liye. High-dimensional sparse TF-IDF matrix → low-dimensional dense representation. Synonymy aur polysemy partially handle karta hai. Topic modeling ka foundation hai.
real_life_example: 1000 documents, 50K vocab → TF-IDF matrix 1000×50K. SVD apply karo → 1000×100 dense matrix. Similar documents close honge. Wikipedia search mein LSA use hota tha semantic matching ke liye, ab neural methods ne replace kar diya.
how_to_answer: LSA: applies SVD to term-document matrix for dimensionality reduction
Input: TF-IDF weighted term-document matrix
SVD decomposes into: U × Σ × V^T
Keep top-k singular values → k-dimensional representation
Captures latent semantic structure: synonyms map nearby
Limitations: linear, bag-of-words assumption, no word order
Precursor to modern embeddings, replaced by neural methods

question: What is topic modeling and how does LDA work?
hinglish_explanation: Topic modeling: documents mein hidden topics discover karna unsupervised way mein. LDA (Latent Dirichlet Allocation): har document mix of topics hai, har topic mix of words hai. Generative model hai - Dirichlet distribution assume karta hai. Interpretable topics milte hain.
real_life_example: News articles pe LDA lagao: Topic 1 (sports): cricket, match, player. Topic 2 (politics): election, BJP, Congress. Topic 3 (tech): AI, startup, funding. Har article ka topic distribution milta hai. News categorization automatically!
how_to_answer: Topic modeling: discover hidden themes in document collection
LDA: each document is mixture of topics, each topic is mixture of words
Generative model with Dirichlet priors on distributions
Hyperparameters: number of topics (k), alpha, beta
Training: variational inference or Gibbs sampling
Output: topic-word distributions + document-topic distributions
Use cases: content organization, trend analysis, recommendation

question: How does TF-IDF compare with learned embeddings for text representation?
hinglish_explanation: TF-IDF: sparse, interpretable, no training needed, word overlap based. Embeddings: dense, semantic similarity capture, training needed. TF-IDF + SVM still strong baseline hai. BERT embeddings best quality but slow/expensive. Choice depends on data size, compute, requirements.
real_life_example: Startup: 500 labeled examples, limited GPU → TF-IDF + Logistic Regression (2 min training, 85% accuracy). Scale-up: 50K examples, GPU available → BERT fine-tuning (hours training, 95% accuracy). Start simple, upgrade when needed!
how_to_answer: TF-IDF: sparse, explicit term matching, no semantic understanding
Embeddings: dense, captures meaning similarity, needs training
TF-IDF advantages: fast, interpretable, no GPU needed, strong baseline
Embeddings advantages: semantic matching, handles synonyms, OOV
TF-IDF fails: 'automobile' vs 'car' (no match)
Embeddings fail: exact keyword matching, rare domain terms
My approach: TF-IDF baseline first, then upgrade to embeddings

question: What is the difference between sparse and dense text representations?
hinglish_explanation: Sparse: mostly zeros, high dimensional (BoW, TF-IDF, one-hot). Dense: all values non-zero, low dimensional (Word2Vec, BERT). Sparse = exact matching, interpretable. Dense = semantic matching, compact. Modern hybrid approaches dono combine karte hain (SPLADE).
real_life_example: Product search: sparse (BM25) 'blue shirt' exact match karega. Dense (SBERT) 'navy top' bhi similar mein laayega. Best: dono combine karo. Hybrid search (Pinecone, Elasticsearch) sparse+dense dono use karta hai.
how_to_answer: Sparse: high-dimensional, mostly zeros (BoW, TF-IDF, one-hot)
Dense: low-dimensional, all values meaningful (embeddings)
Sparse: exact term matching, interpretable, fast with inverted index
Dense: semantic matching, compact storage, ANN search
Sparse limitation: no synonym handling
Dense limitation: may miss exact matches
Hybrid (BM25 + dense): combines benefits of both

question: What is SPLADE and how does it create learned sparse representations?
hinglish_explanation: SPLADE (SParse Lexical AnD Expansion) BERT use karke sparse vectors generate karta hai jo traditional sparse (BM25) aur dense ke benefits combine karta hai. Query/document expansion karta hai - related terms add karta hai. Inverted index pe search possible + semantic understanding.
real_life_example: Query 'laptop repair' → SPLADE expands to include 'computer', 'fix', 'service' implicitly. Better recall than BM25 but still uses inverted index = fast. Naver Search mein production mein use hota hai.
how_to_answer: SPLADE: learned sparse representations using transformer
Uses BERT MLM head to generate term importance weights
Sparse but semantically-aware: expands queries with related terms
Combines BM25-like efficiency with neural semantic understanding
Can use inverted index for fast retrieval
Regularization controls sparsity (FLOPS regularizer)
Competitive with dense retrieval while being more interpretable

question: How does attention mechanism help in text representation?
hinglish_explanation: Attention important words ko zyada weight deta hai representation mein. 'The movie was absolutely fantastic despite poor marketing' - attention 'fantastic' pe zyada focus karega sentiment ke liye. Self-attention (transformer) har word ko har dusre word ke context mein dekhta hai.
real_life_example: Email summarization: long email mein kuch sentences important hain, baaki filler. Attention mechanism automatically important parts identify karta hai aur unhe zyada weight deta hai representation mein. Gmail smart compose aise hi kaam karta hai.
how_to_answer: Attention: dynamically weight tokens based on relevance
Self-attention: each token attends to all other tokens
Creates context-aware representations unlike simple averaging
Enables variable-length input → fixed output with selective focus
Key innovation in transformers: multi-head self-attention
Solves: long-range dependencies, selective information routing
Different attention heads capture different relationships

question: What is document embedding and how is it different from word embedding?
hinglish_explanation: Word embedding: ek word ka vector. Document embedding: pura document (paragraph/page) ka single vector. Challenge: variable length text ko fixed-size vector mein compress karna meaning preserve karke. Doc2Vec, SBERT, USE sab document embeddings dete hain.
real_life_example: Legal document similarity: 50-page contracts compare karne hain. Har contract ka ek 768-dim vector banao (SBERT se). Cosine similarity se similar contracts dhundho. M&A due diligence mein crores ke documents automatically cluster ho jaate hain.
how_to_answer: Word embedding: single word → fixed vector
Document embedding: entire document → fixed vector
Challenge: compress variable-length text preserving meaning
Methods: Doc2Vec, averaged word vectors, SBERT, USE
Hierarchical: word → sentence → paragraph → document
Quality depends on: document length, method, domain
Use cases: similarity, clustering, retrieval, classification

question: What are the limitations of averaging word embeddings for sentence representation?
hinglish_explanation: Simple average word order ignore karta hai - 'dog bites man' = 'man bites dog'. Common words dominate, rare important words dilute ho jaate hain. Negation handle nahi hota - 'not good' ka average 'good' ke close. Long documents mein meaning wash out ho jaata hai.
real_life_example: 'This movie is not good at all' - average embedding positive side pe hoga kyunki 'good', 'movie' positive words hain. Proper sentence encoder like SBERT negation correctly handle karta hai aur negative sentiment capture karta hai.
how_to_answer: Loses word order: 'dog bites man' = 'man bites dog'
Negation problem: 'not good' averages toward 'good'
Common words dominate: function words dilute content words
Long documents: meaning gets washed out in averaging
No compositionality: doesn't capture phrase-level meaning
Mitigation: TF-IDF weighting, SIF (smooth inverse frequency)
Better alternatives: SBERT, USE for quality sentence embeddings

question: What is Smooth Inverse Frequency (SIF) embedding and why does it work well?
hinglish_explanation: SIF simple weighted average hai: weight = a/(a + p(w)) jahan p(w) word frequency hai. Common words (the, is) ka weight kam, rare meaningful words ka weight zyada. Phir first principal component remove karo. Surprisingly SBERT ke close performance deta hai! Simple yet effective.
real_life_example: Without SIF: 'the the the important' mein 'the' dominate karega. SIF se 'the' ka weight almost 0, 'important' ka weight high. Research paper showed SIF beats LSTM baselines. Quick baseline jab SBERT available nahi ho.
how_to_answer: SIF: weighted average with smooth inverse frequency weights
Weight = a/(a + freq(word)), downweights common words
After averaging, remove first principal component (common discourse vector)
Surprisingly effective: competitive with LSTM baselines
Theoretically motivated: random walk model of text generation
Hyperparameter 'a' typically 1e-3 to 1e-4
Best simple baseline before using SBERT

question: What is a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) and why is it suitable for text?
hinglish_explanation: RNN sequential data process karta hai - ek token at a time, previous state remember karta hai. Text naturally sequential hai - word order matters. Hidden state previous context carry karta hai. Problem: vanishing gradient - long sequences mein purani info bhul jaata hai.
real_life_example: Sentence reading: 'The cat that the dog chased ran away' - RNN ek ek word process karta hai, hidden state mein context maintain karta hai. WhatsApp next word prediction initially RNN-based tha. Now transformers ne replace kar diya.
how_to_answer: RNN: processes sequences one step at a time with memory
Hidden state: carries information from previous time steps
h_t = f(W_h * h_{t-1} + W_x * x_t + b)
Natural for text: captures sequential dependencies
Vanishing gradient: hard to learn long-range dependencies
Exploding gradient: mitigated by gradient clipping
Largely replaced by transformers but important to understand

question: What is LSTM and how does it solve the vanishing gradient problem?
hinglish_explanation: LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) mein gates hain: forget gate (kya bhulna hai), input gate (kya naya add karna hai), output gate (kya output dena hai). Cell state highway jaisa hai - information directly flow kar sakti hai bina transformation ke. Isliye long-range dependencies learn hoti hain.
real_life_example: Movie review: 'Despite initial slow pace, weak dialogues, and mediocre acting, the climax was BRILLIANT' - LSTM cell state 'despite' yaad rakhega aur 'brilliant' final sentiment decide karega. RNN 'brilliant' tak pahunchte pahunchte 'despite' bhul jayega.
how_to_answer: LSTM: Long Short-Term Memory with gating mechanism
Three gates: forget (what to discard), input (what to store), output (what to expose)
Cell state: highway for information flow without transformation
Forget gate: σ(W_f·[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_f)
Solves vanishing gradient via direct gradient path through cell state
Can learn dependencies spanning 100+ time steps
Standard for: sequence labeling, text generation before transformers

question: What is GRU and how does it compare to LSTM?
hinglish_explanation: GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit) LSTM ka simplified version hai. Sirf 2 gates: reset gate aur update gate. Cell state aur hidden state merge hain. Fewer parameters = faster training. Performance LSTM ke comparable hai most tasks pe. Choose based on: dataset size aur speed requirements.
real_life_example: Mobile chatbot: GRU prefer karo kyunki LSTM se 33% fewer parameters hain = faster inference phone pe. Accuracy similar hogi. Research papers mein LSTM zyada popular hai but GRU production-friendly hai resource-constrained environments mein.
how_to_answer: GRU: simplified LSTM with 2 gates instead of 3
Update gate: combines forget and input gate of LSTM
Reset gate: controls how much past info to forget
Fewer parameters than LSTM: faster training and inference
No separate cell state: hidden state carries all information
Performance comparable to LSTM on most NLP tasks
Choose GRU for: speed, smaller models; LSTM for: complex dependencies

question: What is a bidirectional RNN and when should you use it?
hinglish_explanation: Bidirectional RNN text ko dono directions se process karta hai: left-to-right aur right-to-left. Har position pe future context bhi available hota hai. NER, POS tagging mein critical hai kyunki word ka meaning dono sides ke context pe depend karta hai. Text generation mein use NAHI ho sakta (future nahi pata).
real_life_example: NER: 'Apple released iPhone' - forward RNN 'Apple' pe sirf left context hai (nothing). Backward RNN 'Apple' pe 'released iPhone' context hai → company. BiRNN dono combine = better prediction. BERT bhi essentially bidirectional hai.
how_to_answer: Processes sequence in both forward and backward directions
Concatenates hidden states from both directions
Each position has access to full left AND right context
Use for: classification, NER, POS tagging, encoding
Do NOT use for: text generation (can't see future)
BiLSTM: standard for sequence labeling before BERT
BERT's MLM is essentially bidirectional attention

question: What is the attention mechanism in sequence-to-sequence models?
hinglish_explanation: Seq2seq mein encoder pura input ek fixed vector mein compress karta hai - information loss. Attention: decoder har step pe encoder ke ALL hidden states dekhta hai aur relevant ones pe focus karta hai. Dynamic weighted sum of encoder states. Machine translation mein revolutionary tha.
real_life_example: English→Hindi translation: 'The cat sat on the mat' translate karte waqt 'बिल्ली' generate karte waqt attention 'cat' pe focus karega, 'बैठी' ke time 'sat' pe. Alignment automatically learn hota hai bina explicit teaching ke.
how_to_answer: Attention allows decoder to focus on relevant encoder states
Instead of single context vector: weighted combination of all states
Score function: dot-product, additive (Bahdanau), multiplicative (Luong)
Alignment weights show which input words matter for each output
Solves information bottleneck of fixed-size encoder vector
Enables better long-sentence translation
Foundation that led to Transformer architecture

question: What is the encoder-decoder architecture?
hinglish_explanation: Encoder input sequence ko fixed representation mein convert karta hai. Decoder us representation se output sequence generate karta hai. Variable-length input → variable-length output. Machine translation, summarization, QA sab encoder-decoder hain. Transformer bhi encoder-decoder hai (T5, BART).
real_life_example: Google Translate: encoder English sentence padhta hai → representation. Decoder Hindi sentence generate karta hai word by word. Summarization: encoder full article → decoder short summary. Chatbot: encoder user message → decoder response.
how_to_answer: Two-part architecture: encoder reads input, decoder generates output
Encoder: processes input sequence → context representation
Decoder: generates output sequence from context, one token at a time
Handles variable-length input to variable-length output
Original: LSTM encoder + LSTM decoder with attention
Modern: Transformer encoder + Transformer decoder (T5, BART)
Use cases: translation, summarization, QA, dialogue

question: What is beam search and how does it improve text generation?
hinglish_explanation: Greedy decoding: har step pe best word pick karo - locally optimal but globally suboptimal. Beam search: top-k (beam width) candidates maintain karo har step pe. Final mein best complete sequence choose karo. Better quality generation but slower. Beam width=4-5 common hai.
real_life_example: Translation: 'I am' ke baad greedy: 'I am going' pick karega. Beam search: 'I am going', 'I am planning', 'I am about to' sab explore karega parallel mein, best complete translation choose karega. Google Translate beam search use karta hai.
how_to_answer: Beam search: maintain top-k candidates at each decoding step
Greedy: pick best token each step - fast but suboptimal
Beam width (k): number of candidates maintained (4-5 typical)
Score: log probability of sequence, length-normalized
Higher beam = better quality but slower and more memory
Not guaranteed optimal but practically much better than greedy
Used in: MT, summarization, speech recognition

question: What is teacher forcing in sequence model training?
hinglish_explanation: Training mein decoder ko previous step ka actual correct token dete hain (teacher forces correct input) instead of model's own prediction. Training fast aur stable hoti hai. Problem: exposure bias - training mein hamesha correct input mila, inference mein model ke own errors propagate hote hain.
real_life_example: Translation training: 'मैं जा रहा हूँ' generate karna hai. Teacher forcing: har step pe actual correct Hindi word dete hain as input. Without: agar model 'मैं' ke baad galat word generate kare, error accumulate hoga. Scheduled sampling gradually teacher forcing reduce karta hai.
how_to_answer: Teacher forcing: use ground truth as decoder input during training
Without: use model's own previous prediction as input
Advantage: faster convergence, stable training
Disadvantage: exposure bias (train-test mismatch)
At inference: no ground truth available, must use own predictions
Scheduled sampling: gradually reduce teacher forcing ratio
Curriculum learning: start with full TF, reduce over training

question: What is sequence labeling and what are its applications?
hinglish_explanation: Sequence labeling: input sequence ke har token ko ek label assign karna. NER: har word ko entity type. POS: har word ko grammatical category. Chunking: har word ko phrase type. Output sequence same length hai input ke. BiLSTM-CRF traditional SOTA tha, ab BERT-based models hain.
real_life_example: NER on 'Virat Kohli scored century at Wankhede' → [B-PER, I-PER, O, O, O, B-LOC]. POS: [NNP, NNP, VBD, NN, IN, NNP]. Banking: transaction parsing 'Paid 500 to Flipkart on 15th' → amount, merchant, date extraction.
how_to_answer: Assign label to each token in input sequence
Output length = input length (unlike seq2seq)
Applications: NER, POS tagging, chunking, slot filling
Tagging schemes: BIO, BIOES for entity boundaries
Traditional: BiLSTM-CRF (captures label dependencies)
Modern: BERT + token classification head
Evaluation: entity-level F1 for NER, token accuracy for POS

question: What is the vanishing gradient problem and how does it affect NLP?
hinglish_explanation: Long sequences mein gradient back-propagate karte karte bahut chhota ho jaata hai (vanish). Early layers barely update hoti hain. RNN 'The man who went to the store and bought groceries then came home and cooked dinner was tired' - 'man' aur 'tired' ka connection learn nahi ho paata.
real_life_example: Long document classification: 1000 word review mein beginning ki info end tak propagate nahi hoti vanilla RNN mein. Solutions: LSTM/GRU (gating), Transformer (direct connections), Residual connections. Modern architectures ne ye problem largely solve kar di.
how_to_answer: Gradients shrink exponentially during backpropagation through time
Effect: can't learn long-range dependencies in sequences
Cause: repeated multiplication of small gradient values
RNN: practical limit ~10-20 steps for learning dependencies
Solutions: LSTM/GRU (gating mechanism preserves gradients)
Transformers: direct connections, no sequential bottleneck
Other fixes: gradient clipping, residual connections, layer norm

question: What is sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) modeling?
hinglish_explanation: Seq2seq: variable-length input sequence → variable-length output sequence. Encoder-decoder architecture use hota hai. Translation (English→Hindi), summarization (long→short), chatbot (question→answer). Input aur output lengths different ho sakte hain.
real_life_example: Chatbot: User 'What is the weather in Delhi?' (7 tokens) → Bot 'It is 42 degrees and sunny in Delhi today' (10 tokens). Different lengths! Seq2seq handles this naturally. Code: text description → code generation bhi seq2seq hai.
how_to_answer: Maps input sequence to output sequence of potentially different length
Architecture: encoder processes input, decoder generates output
Original: LSTM/GRU based with attention
Modern: Transformer-based (T5, BART, mBART)
Applications: translation, summarization, QA, dialogue
Training: teacher forcing with cross-entropy loss
Inference: beam search or sampling for generation

question: What is the CRF layer and why is it added on top of BiLSTM for NER?
hinglish_explanation: BiLSTM har token independently classify karta hai - 'I-PER' ke baad 'B-LOC' aa sakta hai (invalid!). CRF (Conditional Random Field) transition constraints learn karta hai - valid sequences hi produce karega. BiLSTM-CRF globally optimal label sequence deta hai using Viterbi decoding.
real_life_example: NER without CRF: 'Narendra Modi' → [B-PER, B-PER] (wrong! should be B-PER, I-PER). CRF ensures valid transitions: B-PER ke baad I-PER hi aa sakta hai same entity ka. Like grammar rules for labels.
how_to_answer: CRF: models dependencies between adjacent labels
BiLSTM alone: classifies each token independently
Problem: may produce invalid label sequences (I-PER after B-ORG)
CRF layer: learns valid transition probabilities between labels
Viterbi algorithm: finds globally optimal label sequence
BiLSTM-CRF: was SOTA for NER before BERT
BERT + CRF: marginal improvement, often BERT alone is sufficient

question: What are the differences between RNN, LSTM, and Transformer architectures?
hinglish_explanation: RNN: simple, vanishing gradient. LSTM: gates solve gradient issue, sequential (slow). Transformer: parallel processing, self-attention, handles long-range dependencies best. Training speed: Transformer >> LSTM >> RNN. Quality: Transformer > LSTM > RNN. Transformers won on all fronts.
real_life_example: 1000 word document process: RNN = 1000 sequential steps. LSTM = 1000 steps (better quality). Transformer = parallel all at once + attention across all positions. GPU pe Transformer 10-100x faster train hota hai LSTM se. Isliye ab sab Transformer use karte hain.
how_to_answer: RNN: sequential, vanishing gradient, simple but limited
LSTM: gating solves gradient, still sequential processing
Transformer: parallel, self-attention, best long-range modeling
Speed: Transformer parallelizes; RNN/LSTM inherently sequential
Memory: Transformer O(n²) attention; LSTM O(n) but sequential
Modern NLP: Transformers dominate all benchmarks
RNN/LSTM still useful for: streaming, low-resource, edge devices

question: What is the copy mechanism in sequence-to-sequence models?
hinglish_explanation: Standard seq2seq sirf vocab se words generate kar sakta hai. Copy mechanism input se directly words copy kar sakta hai output mein. Rare words, names, numbers ke liye essential hai. Pointer network/CopyNet input pe point karke words copy karta hai. Summarization mein critical hai.
real_life_example: Summarization: 'Tata Motors announced Q3 revenue of ₹97,000 crores' - 'Tata Motors' aur '₹97,000 crores' vocab mein nahi honge but copy mechanism directly input se copy kar sakta hai. Names/numbers faithfully reproduce hote hain.
how_to_answer: Copy mechanism: allows model to copy tokens directly from input
Pointer Network: points to input positions for copying
Pointer-Generator: hybrid - generate from vocab OR copy from input
Essential for: proper nouns, numbers, rare words in output
Without copy: OOV words impossible to generate correctly
Used in: abstractive summarization, data-to-text generation
PGN (Pointer Generator Network) popular for summarization

question: What is packed padding in RNN-based models and why is it important?
hinglish_explanation: Batch mein sentences different lengths ki hoti hain. Padding: sab ko same length karo (zeros add). Problem: RNN padded zeros pe bhi compute waste karti hai. Packed sequences: actual lengths batao, RNN sirf real tokens process kare. PyTorch mein pack_padded_sequence use hota hai.
real_life_example: Batch: ['I love NLP' (3 words), 'Hi' (1 word)]. Padding: ['I love NLP', 'Hi PAD PAD']. Without packing: RNN 'Hi PAD PAD' pe 3 steps run karega uselessly. Packing: RNN 'Hi' ke baad stop. 30-40% training speedup possible!
how_to_answer: Padding: make all sequences same length with PAD tokens
Problem: RNN computes over PAD tokens wastefully
Packed sequences: tell model actual lengths, skip padding
PyTorch: pack_padded_sequence before RNN, pad_packed_sequence after
Sort batch by length (descending) for efficient packing
Speedup: 20-40% faster training with packing
Also important for correct loss computation (ignore PAD in loss)

question: What is the difference between autoregressive and non-autoregressive generation?
hinglish_explanation: Autoregressive: ek token at a time generate, previous tokens pe conditioned (GPT). Non-autoregressive: sab tokens simultaneously generate (parallel). AR: better quality, slow. NAR: faster, lower quality. Translation mein NAR 10-15x faster hai acceptable quality drop ke saath.
real_life_example: GPT typing: ek ek word generate hota hai sequentially (autoregressive). Real-time translation app mein 500ms latency unacceptable - NAR model sab words parallel generate = 50ms. Quality thodi kam but speed critical applications ke liye NAR useful hai.
how_to_answer: Autoregressive (AR): generate one token at a time, left-to-right
Non-autoregressive (NAR): generate all tokens simultaneously
NAR: P(y) = P(y1)×P(y2)×P(y3)×... (independent)
AR: better quality due to token dependencies captured
NAR: 10-15x faster but lower quality (multi-modality problem)
Hybrid: iterative NAR (few iterations of refinement)

question: What is word-level vs character-level modeling in NLP?
hinglish_explanation: Word-level: vocabulary of words (50K+), each word = one token. Character-level: vocabulary sirf characters (100-200), word character by character generate. Character-level OOV problem nahi hai but sequences bahut long ho jaati hain. Subword (BPE) best of both worlds hai.
real_life_example: Name generation: character-level model 'R-a-m-e-s-h' generate karta hai character by character. Word-level model sirf known names generate kar sakta hai. Typo correction bhi character-level model better handle karta hai. But training slow hai long sequences ki wajah se.
how_to_answer: Word-level: each word is one token, large vocabulary (50K+)
Character-level: each character is one token, tiny vocab (~200)
Word: shorter sequences, meaningful units, OOV problem
Character: no OOV, morphology capture, but very long sequences
Character: slower training due to long sequences
Subword: compromise between word and character level
Modern standard: subword tokenization (BPE/WordPiece)

question: What is dropout in RNNs and how is it different from standard dropout?
hinglish_explanation: Standard dropout: random neurons off har step pe (different mask). RNN mein ye kaam nahi karta - temporal connections break ho jaate hain. Variational dropout: same mask use karo har time step pe. Har layer ke beech dropout lagao, same timestep pe nahi. Zoneout LSTM-specific variant hai.
real_life_example: LSTM overfitting ho raha hai training data pe. Standard dropout lagao = unstable training. Variational dropout (same mask across time) lagao = proper regularization without breaking temporal flow. PyTorch LSTM mein dropout parameter inter-layer dropout hai.
how_to_answer: Standard dropout in RNN: different mask each timestep - harmful
Variational/locked dropout: same mask across all timesteps
Apply between layers, not within recurrence
PyTorch LSTM dropout param: applies between stacked layers
Zoneout: randomly maintain previous hidden state (LSTM-specific)
DropConnect: drop weights instead of activations
Typical values: 0.2-0.5 depending on model size

question: What is the difference between Bahdanau and Luong attention?
hinglish_explanation: Bahdanau (additive): concat-based, uses previous decoder state for attention. Luong (multiplicative): dot-product based, uses current decoder state. Luong simpler aur faster hai. Bahdanau pehle aaya (2014), Luong (2015) ne simplify kiya. Transformer ka attention Luong-style (scaled dot-product) hai.
real_life_example: Machine translation research: Bahdanau paper ne attention introduce kiya, Luong ne 3 variants diye (dot, general, concat). Practice mein Luong dot-product fastest hai aur Transformer mein scaled version use hota hai. Interview mein dono ka difference puchte hain.
how_to_answer: Bahdanau (2014): additive attention, score = v^T × tanh(W[h_s; h_t])
Luong (2015): multiplicative, score = h_s^T × W × h_t (or just dot)
Bahdanau: uses h_{t-1} (previous decoder state) for attention
Luong: uses h_t (current decoder state) for attention
Luong variants: dot product, general (learnable matrix), concat
Dot product: fastest, no learnable parameters
Transformer uses scaled dot-product (Luong-style): Q×K^T/√d

question: What is text generation with temperature and top-k/top-p sampling?
hinglish_explanation: Temperature: logits divide karo temperature se. Low temp (0.1) = confident/repetitive. High temp (1.5) = creative/random. Top-k: sirf top k probable words mein se sample karo. Top-p (nucleus): cumulative probability p tak ke words mein se sample. Combination = controllable generation.
real_life_example: ChatGPT mein temperature setting: code generation ke liye low temperature (0.2) = precise/deterministic. Creative writing ke liye high temperature (0.8) = diverse/creative. top-p=0.9 typical setting hai jo boring repetition avoid karta hai.
how_to_answer: Temperature: scales logits before softmax, controls randomness
Low temp (<0.5): peaked distribution, deterministic output
High temp (>1): flat distribution, more random/creative
Top-k: sample only from k most likely tokens
Top-p (nucleus): sample from smallest set with cumulative prob ≥ p
Combine: temperature + top-p most common in practice
ChatGPT default: temperature=0.7, top-p=1.0 approximately

question: What is self-attention and how does it work in Transformers?
hinglish_explanation: Self-attention: har token apne sequence ke har dusre token ko attend karta hai. Q (query), K (key), V (value) matrices learn hoti hain. Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T/√d)V. Har word ka representation pura sentence consider karke banta hai. Parallel computation possible!
real_life_example: 'The animal didn't cross the street because it was too wide' - 'it' kya refer karta hai? Self-attention 'it' ke Q ko 'street' ke K ke saath high score dega → 'it'='street' samajh jayega. Long-range reference resolve!
how_to_answer: Self-attention: each token attends to all tokens in the sequence
Compute Q (query), K (key), V (value) from input embeddings
